topics.title: Interview Framework
topics.description: Five phases to structure any system design interview. For 3-6 YOE backend roles the bar is: structure the conversation, know the building blocks, reason about trade-offs out loud. Nobody expects Google-scale war stories.

steps.title: 1. Requirements (5 min)
steps.description: Functional (what must it do) plus non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Ask for numbers: DAU, reads/writes ratio, payload sizes.

steps.title: 2. Back-of-envelope estimates (3 min)
steps.description: Size the system roughly. Do not be precise, be reasonable.

steps.title: 3. High-level design (10 min)
steps.description: Draw the boxes and walk through the main read path and the main write path.

steps.title: 4. Deep dives (15 min)
steps.description: The interviewer picks, or you offer: data model, scaling the bottleneck, failure handling.

steps.title: 5. Wrap-up
steps.description: Bottlenecks, single points of failure, what you would monitor, what you would do next.

topics.diagram: client → LB → stateless services → cache → DB (+ queue for async work)

topics.title: Load Balancing
topics.description: Spread traffic across interchangeable instances. Health checks plus statelessness are what make horizontal scaling work.

layers.title: L7
layers.description: HTTP-aware: routing by path or header, TLS termination.

algorithms: Consistent hashing — sticky routing without shared state
topics.health_checks: Health checks eject bad instances. This plus statelessness equals horizontal scaling.
topics.stateless_services: Keep session state out of app servers (JWT, or a session store in Redis) so any instance can serve any request, then scale by adding instances behind the load balancer.

topics.title: Caching
topics.description: Cache-aside is the pattern you will be asked about: read, miss, load from the database, put in the cache with a TTL.

topics.title: Database Scaling
topics.description: Escalate in this order. Each step is cheaper and less disruptive than the one after it.

escalation_ladder.title: 2. Read replicas
escalation_ladder.description: Offload reads. Mention replication lag: the read-your-own-writes problem, solved by routing a user's reads to the primary briefly after a write.

escalation_ladder.title: 4. Partitioning / sharding
escalation_ladder.description: Split by key (user_id hash or range). Costs: cross-shard queries, resharding pain, no global transactions. Consistent hashing limits data movement when adding shards.

escalation_ladder.title: 5. Polyglot persistence
escalation_ladder.description: Move specific workloads to fitting stores: search to Elasticsearch, counters to Redis, events to Kafka.

topics.title: SQL vs NoSQL
topics.description: Relational by default: transactions, joins, mature tooling.
topics.the_line_to_use: Say "PostgreSQL until proven otherwise" — it is a respected answer.

topics.title: Queues & Async
topics.description: Decouple producers from consumers, absorb spikes, retry safely.

queue_vs_log.title: Queue — SQS, RabbitMQ
queue_vs_log.description: Competing consumers. The message is deleted once handled.

queue_vs_log.title: Log — Kafka
queue_vs_log.description: Replayable, ordered per partition, multiple consumer groups.

topics.title: CAP & Consistency
topics.description: Under a network Partition you choose Consistency (reject writes) or Availability (serve possibly stale data).
topics.how_to_apply_it: Most web features tolerate eventual consistency; money movement does not. Say which parts of your design need which.

topics.title: Idempotency
topics.description: Network retries mean duplicates. Every retry needs an idempotency story.
techniques: Idempotency keys — client-generated UUID, server dedupes

topics.title: Rate Limiting
topics.description: Protect downstream capacity and shed abusive traffic at the edge.
algorithms: Token bucket — burst-friendly, the default answer
topics.implementation: Store counters in Redis: atomic INCR plus EXPIRE, or a Lua script.

topics.title: Observability
topics.description: What you would monitor, named concretely, is a strong wrap-up answer.
pillars: Metrics — Prometheus / Micrometer, RED: rate, errors, duration

topics.title: Classic Designs
topics.description: Thirty-second versions of the walkthroughs that come up most often.

walkthroughs.title: URL Shortener
walkthroughs.write: Generate an ID (base62 of a sequence, or snowflake) and store code to long_url, then return the short link.
walkthroughs.read: Read path dominates 100:1 — cache hot codes in Redis; 301 redirect, or 302 if you want analytics.
walkthroughs.scale: Read replicas or a DynamoDB-style key-value store; codes are shard-friendly.
walkthroughs.note: Using a sequence avoids the hashing collision debate.

walkthroughs.title: Rate Limiter as a Service
walkthroughs.core: Token bucket per API key in Redis, with a Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement.
walkthroughs.optimization: A local in-memory pre-filter cuts Redis load.

walkthroughs.title: Notification Service
walkthroughs.ingest: API accepts the request, validates it, publishes to a Kafka topic per channel (email, SMS, push).
walkthroughs.workers: Consume and call providers (SendGrid, Twilio) with retries and a dead-letter queue.
walkthroughs.safeguards: Idempotency key per notification prevents duplicates; template service; per-user rate caps and preference checks.

walkthroughs.title: News Feed
walkthroughs.write: Fan-out-on-write to followers' feed caches (Redis lists), but fan-out-on-read for celebrities — a hybrid.
walkthroughs.read: Merge the cached feed with celebrity posts, hydrate post details, paginate by cursor rather than offset.

walkthroughs.title: Chat and Presence
walkthroughs.transport: WebSockets on gateway servers, sticky by user; messages flow through Kafka.
walkthroughs.extras: Delivery receipts as separate lightweight events; presence via heartbeat plus TTL keys in Redis.

topics.title: Trade-off Phrases
topics.description: Lines that score points when you say them out loud.
phrases: I'll start simple and only shard when a single primary can't hold the write load.
This queue makes the system eventually consistent — acceptable here because the user sees their own write from the cache.
I'd rather over-provision Redis than add a cache layer I can't invalidate correctly.
Every retry needs an idempotency story; here it's the unique constraint on (user_id, request_id).

topics.title: Interview Questions
topics.description: Rehearsed answers to the questions this note prepares for.

questions.question: How would you scale a Spring Boot monolith that's slowing down?
questions.answer: Measure first (APM, slow query log). Then: indexes and queries, cache hot reads, read replicas, extract the truly hot module behind an API or a queue. Microservices are the last step, not the first — this ordering signals seniority.

questions.question: How do you keep cache and database consistent?
questions.answer: Cache-aside with a TTL as the safety net. On writes, update the database then delete (not update) the cache key; accept a small stale window, or use versioned keys. Mention the classic race and why delete-after-write plus TTL bounds the damage.

questions.question: Strong vs eventual consistency — how do you choose?
questions.answer: Ask what breaks if a reader sees data 2 seconds old. Payments and inventory reservation need strong consistency (single primary, transactions). Feeds, counters and analytics are fine with eventual.

questions.question: What's a single point of failure in your design and how do you remove it?
questions.answer: Walk each tier: load balancer (managed or an HA pair), services (N instances, multi-AZ), cache (Redis replicas plus sentinel or cluster), database (primary with automated failover), queue (replicated brokers).
